summary: Analyzes the security and privacy implications of transient numeric identifiers in IETF protocols, categorizes them by their interoperability needs, and gives advice on algorithms that satisfy those needs while limiting security and privacy harm.

plainLanguage.summary: Many protocols carry a number that only has to be unique for a while, such as a packet ID or a first sequence number. Picking one is easy; picking one that is hard to guess is harder, because some protocols need the number to increase steadily and others do not. This RFC sorts these numbers into four kinds, says what each kind needs, and gives a tested algorithm for each one with its weaknesses spelled out.

questions: how to generate transient numeric identifiers
algorithms for sequence numbers and ids
difference between soft and hard failure
what are the four categories of transient numeric identifier
subtitle: How to pick transient identifiers so that they stay unique without becoming predictable.

tldr.problem: Different transient numeric identifiers have different requirements and different consequences when they collide, and without guidance protocol designers and implementers keep choosing weak algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9415 sorts identifiers into four categories based on what they must guarantee and what a collision costs, then gives sample algorithms for each category, from plain randomisation through keyed hash functions, with the trade-offs of each spelled out.
tldr.outcome: Designers now have tested algorithms and their limits to choose from, and a companion document, RFC 9416, makes stating the requirements, assessing the risk and recommending an algorithm mandatory in new IETF specifications.

today: RFC 9415 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the reference for algorithm choice, with RFC 9414 giving the historical motivation and RFC 9416 making the guidance normative for new IETF specifications.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
Networking protocols use a variety of transient numeric identifiers for different protocol objects: IPv4 and IPv6 Identification values, IPv6 Interface Identifiers, transport-protocol ephemeral port numbers, TCP Initial Sequence Numbers, NTP Reference IDs and DNS IDs. These identifiers usually have requirements, such as uniqueness during a specified period, that must be met without negative interoperability consequences and without an associated failure severity when they are not met.

For more than 30 years a large number of implementations of IETF protocols have been subject to attacks ranging from denial of service and data injection to information leakage that could be exploited for pervasive monitoring. The root cause has in many cases been the poor selection of transient numeric identifiers, usually as a result of insufficient or misleading specifications. Implementations have been hit by predictable IPv4 and IPv6 Identification values, predictable IPv6 interface identifiers, predictable ephemeral port numbers, predictable TCP initial sequence numbers, predictable initial timestamps in the TCP timestamps option, and predictable DNS IDs. Recent history indicates that when new protocols are standardized or new implementations are produced, the security and privacy properties of these identifiers tend to be overlooked.

The document notes that cryptographic techniques may readily mitigate some of the issues arising from predictable identifiers: cryptographic authentication can mitigate data injection attacks even with predictable sequence numbers. However, use of flawed algorithms such as global counters can still result in information leakage even when cryptographic techniques are employed.

This document surveys the identifiers used in various IETF protocols, categorizes them by their interoperability requirements and the associated failure severity when those requirements are not met, advises on algorithms that could be used for each category while minimizing negative security and privacy implications, and analyses several algorithms that have been used in real implementations. The document represents the consensus of the Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The companion document records why this matters, with three decades of examples. This one answers the practical question: given that you need a number that is unique for a while, how should you pick it? The answer depends on what else the protocol requires of the number and on how bad a collision would be.

sections.title: Terms and the Threat Model
sections.content:
A transient numeric identifier is a data object in a protocol specification that can be used to definitely distinguish a protocol object, such as a datagram, network interface, transport-protocol endpoint or session, from all other objects of the same type in a given context. These identifiers are usually defined as a series of bits and represented using integer values, and are typically dynamically selected, as opposed to statically assigned numeric identifiers. Different identifiers may have additional requirements depending on their specific use in a protocol.

Two levels of failure severity are used. A soft failure is a recoverable condition in which a protocol does not operate in the prescribed manner but normal operation resumes automatically in a short period of time; a simple packet loss that is recovered by a retransmission is an example. A hard failure is a non-recoverable condition in which a protocol does not operate in the prescribed manner, or operates with excessive degradation of service; an established TCP connection aborted by an error condition is an example, since the protocol enters a state from which normal operation cannot resume. Severity is judged from the point of view of the protocol in question, and the severity seen by an application above may differ: a TCP connection that is aborted might have no effect on the application if it can simply reconnect, or it might be a hard failure at the application too.

On-path attacks are not considered. The attacker is assumed not to have physical or logical access to the systems being attacked and can only observe traffic explicitly directed to it. The attacker cannot observe traffic between the sender and the receiver of a target protocol, but may interact with any of these entities, for example by sending traffic to them to sample the identifiers those hosts use when talking to the attacker. Applied to TCP initial sequence numbers, the attacker cannot capture the traffic of a connection between two other hosts but can establish a connection with either of them to sample the sequence numbers it uses. Applied to IPv6 interface identifiers, the attacker may learn a victim's address when the victim talks to an attacker-operated server, and can then track the host by probing a set of addresses built from target prefixes and the learned interface identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things are being sorted here. The first is what the number has to do: be unique, or be unique and stable, or be unique and increasing. The second is what happens when it goes wrong: a lost packet that gets retransmitted is a soft failure, while a connection that cannot resume is a hard one. The attacker in this document never sees your traffic to anyone else; it only talks to you directly and studies what your machine sends back.

sections.title: Four Categories of Identifier
sections.content:
The document surveys the identifiers used in popular protocols, which together cover the combinations of interoperability requirement and failure severity found at different layers.

  • The IPv6 Identification must be unique for an address pair, and its severity is soft or hard: a single collision would simply drop a packet, but repeated collisions at high data rates might cause self-propagating collisions and a hard failure.
  • The IPv6 Interface Identifier must be unique and stable within an IPv6 prefix, with a soft failure. Duplicate Address Detection lets a collision be detected and recovered.
  • The TCP Initial Sequence Number must be monotonically increasing, with a hard failure. In theory there is no interoperability requirement, since the TIME-WAIT state and TCP's quiet time handle old segments, but a widespread optimization allows a new incarnation of a connection when the incoming sequence number is larger than the last one seen in that direction, so increasing sequence numbers keep that optimization working.
  • The TCP initial timestamp has the same requirement and severity, for the same reason.
  • The TCP ephemeral port must be unique for a connection, with a hard failure.
  • The IPv6 Flow Label and the DNS ID need only be unique, with no failure severity: a repeated flow label only causes two flows to be multiplexed onto the same link if it happens deterministically, and a repeated DNS ID only costs a small performance penalty because the response is discarded when it turns out not to answer the query.

From that survey the document derives four categories. Category 1 is uniqueness with soft failure, with the IPv6 Flow Label and DNS ID as samples. Category 2 is uniqueness with hard failure, with the IPv6 Identification and the TCP ephemeral port. Category 3 is uniqueness that is stable within a context, with soft failure, with the IPv6 Interface Identifier. Category 4 is uniqueness that is monotonically increasing within a context, with hard failure, with the TCP initial sequence number and the TCP initial timestamp. Category 4 can be seen as a generalisation of Category 3, in which a monotonically increasing element is added to a stable one, so the same algorithm can serve both with the right parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The categories come from two questions: what must the number do, and what happens if it repeats. A DNS query ID only has to be unique, and a repeat costs nothing much. A TCP port number has to be unique for the life of the connection, and a repeat breaks the connection. A TCP sequence number has to increase, because stacks use that to decide a new connection is really new.

sections.title: Random Algorithms for Simple Categories
sections.content:
For Category 1, uniqueness with soft failure, the requirement can be met with a pseudorandom number generator. Most systems offer one, but many such implementations are not cryptographically secure and so may be statistically biased or open to adversarial influence; the ISO C rand(3) function is not cryptographically secure. A number of systems provide a Cryptographically Secure PRNG, which guarantees high entropy, unpredictability and a good statistical distribution: GNU/Linux offers getentropy(3) and OpenBSD offers arc4random(3) and arc4random_uniform(3). Where these are available they should be preferred over POSIX random(3) or ISO C rand(3). Where a cryptographically secure generator is not readily available for a Category 1 identifier, a security and privacy assessment of using a regular generator should be performed to support the decision.

Because collisions in this category only lead to soft failures, the algorithm often does not need to check whether a selected identifier is suitable at all. When simultaneous use of a value is undesirable and the implementation notices it, the implementation may take the next available identifier in sequence, or select another random number.

The first algorithm picks a random starting value and then walks forward to the next available identifier when it finds one unsuitable. It is biased towards the first available identifier after a run of unavailable ones: if the local list of unsuitable port numbers is long, an attacker may have a significantly better chance of guessing the port. The second algorithm picks a fresh random number every time, which gives a more uniform distribution but may fail to find a value even when suitable ones exist, and so may need many more iterations when the implementation keeps local state of used values. Implementations that keep such state tend to prefer the first algorithm.

Both algorithms warn about the same trap: taking the output of the generator modulo the size of the identifier range can change its distribution, so rejection sampling should be used to preserve uniformity. Assuming the randomness requirements for the generator are met, neither algorithm suffers from the issues analysed later in the document.

For Category 2, uniqueness with hard failure, the simplest approach is to reduce the reuse frequency by generating identifiers with a monotonically increasing function, so any of the Category 4 algorithms can be used. Where suitability can be definitely assessed by the local system, the Category 1 algorithms can be used as well. That does not hold for TCP ephemeral ports or TCP initial sequence numbers, because a value that looks suitable locally may be unsuitable to the remote system, which may hold state associated with it.
sections.plainLanguage: When all you need is that the number is unlikely to repeat, use a good random source, preferably the operating system's cryptographically secure one. Two ways of handling a clash are given: step to the next free number, or draw again. Stepping forward is faster but makes the values predictable in a cluster of already-used numbers, which is exactly the weakness attackers look for. The hard-failure category cannot always use plain randomness, because only the local system can tell whether a value is really free.

sections.title: Keyed Algorithms for Stable and Increasing Identifiers
sections.content:
Category 3 needs identifiers that are stable for a given context but change when the context changes. Rather than storing a value per context in memory, the algorithm computes it: it takes a pseudorandom function F(CONTEXT, retry, secret_key), reduces the result modulo the identifier range, and if the candidate is unsuitable increments the retry counter and recomputes. The function must not be computable from outside without the secret key, must be difficult to reverse even given samples of its output and control of the other inputs, and should produce at least as many bits as the identifier needs. Two options are given: SipHash-2-4 with a 128-bit key and 64-bit output, and BLAKE3 with a 256-bit key and arbitrary-length output. Alternatively the function could be a keyed hash message authentication code, with HMAC-SHA-256 as one option; HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 are not recommended. The result of the function is no more secure than the secret key, which must be unknown to the attacker, of a reasonable length and stable for the given context, otherwise the stability property is lost. For IPv6 interface identifiers the context would be the concatenation of the network interface index and the stateless address autoconfiguration prefix.

Collisions are recovered by incrementing the retry variable, up to a maximum number of retries, but the recovered identifier then no longer stays constant for the context. That is normally acceptable when the probability of a collision is small. Identifiers generated this way do allow network activity correlation and fingerprinting within the context, which is essentially the design goal of this category.

Category 4 needs identifiers that increase monotonically for each context. Three algorithms are given. The per-context counter keeps a counter for each context, initialised to a random value and incremented each time an identifier is needed, so the values are unpredictable to an off-path attacker. The drawback is that the implementation must store a counter per context in memory; if a counter is removed by resource management, the last value is lost and the recreated counter starts again from a random value, which can produce reuse or collision. Keeping one counter for every possible context may also be too onerous in memory.

The simple PRF-based algorithm replaces the stored counters with a computed offset per context, from F(CONTEXT, secret_key), plus a single global counter that is added to the offset. The trade-off is information leakage: because all contexts share one counter, an attacker that can make a client open connections to it can subtract consecutive source port values and learn how many connections the victim opened overall in that time. Small random increments instead of a constant one mitigate this partly.

The double-PRF algorithm splits the increment space into buckets. It keeps an array of random values and uses a second pseudorandom function G(CONTEXT, secret_key2) to pick which bucket a context uses, so identifiers for one context do not always shift the sequences of others. The size of the array does not limit the number of sequences; it separates the increment space. An attacker can still analyse traffic within a bucket it has visibility into, but the ability to do so is much reduced, and it can be reduced further with a larger array or with random increments.
sections.plainLanguage: When the number must stay the same for a given context, the system derives it from a keyed hash of the context rather than storing it, so the same context always yields the same value and nobody else can predict it. When the number must also increase, there is a counter on top of that derived value. The trade-off is that a shared counter leaks how many numbers have been handed out, which is why the last algorithm splits the counting space into buckets.

sections.title: The Vulnerabilities and What to Avoid
sections.content:
The document analyses seven classes of vulnerability.

  • Network activity correlation. An identifier that is predictable within a context allows activity to be correlated within it. A stable per-network IPv6 interface identifier allows correlation within a network, while a constant one that stays the same across networks also allows host tracking. An implementation that generates TCP initial sequence numbers with a global counter can be fingerprinted across networks.
  • Information leakage. Identifiers are often generated as a randomised offset for a context plus a monotonically increasing function. The increasing part leaks even when the offset is secret: a per-destination offset with a global counter leaks the total number of outgoing connections, and an offset per address pair with a global counter leaks the number of fragmented packets sent.
  • Fingerprinting. An attacker can sample identifiers and infer the algorithm and its parameters, which may reveal the operating system vendor, type and version. Evading stack fingerprinting is difficult because each protocol has many parameters. Where possible, algorithms that produce no particular pattern should be preferred.
  • Exploitation of the semantics of identifiers. Identifiers that are not semantically opaque are more predictable: a MAC address contains an Organizationally Unique Identifier that may name the vendor, which helps an attacker guessing addresses.
  • Exploitation of collisions. A collision can have hard failure severity, or become one if an attacker can cause collisions deterministically one after another; predictable IP identification values open the door to denial-of-service attacks.
  • Injection attacks. Some protocols use sequence numbers to validate incoming packets, with no built-in cryptographic mechanism, so they are open to injection. Unpredictable sequence numbers are a completely ineffective mitigation against on-path injection and mostly ineffective against blind injection. Cryptographic mitigations are better, but many legacy protocols treat them as optional: TLS protects the application protocol but does nothing about a TCP connection-reset attack, and SEND still relies on successful IPv6 fragment reassembly when its packets do not fit the link MTU.
  • Cryptanalysis. Algorithms that rely on pseudorandom functions can be broken if the function is weak or the key is the wrong size. Overloading the semantics of the secret key can make the cryptanalysis trivial, and one described implementation used 32 bits of a kernel address as the key, so breaking it also bypasses address space layout randomization.

Two further warnings apply to the algorithms themselves. Many implementations adapt the length of a generator's output with a modulo operator, which changes its distribution: an identifier taken as random() % 50000 from a 16-bit uniform generator gives values 0 to 15535 twice as often as 15536 to 49999. The effect is reduced when the generator produces output much longer than the modulo implies, and rejection sampling preserves uniformity. Using algorithms other than generators for Category 1 identifiers is discouraged.

The appendix lists techniques with known issues. The predictable linear identifier algorithm produces a sequence by adding a constant increment, and was used in a number of operating systems for IP identifiers and ephemeral ports; learning one value lets an attacker infer past values and predict future ones, and sampling two values reveals how many identifiers were generated in between. A counter initialised to a known value leaks more, such as the number of fragmented datagrams sent or the system uptime in the case of TCP timestamps. The random-increments algorithm, which adds a random increment of up to a fixed bound to a randomly initialised counter, sits between plain randomisation and a predictable sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: There are seven ways this goes wrong, from simply revealing that two connections belong to the same device, through leaking how busy a host is, to letting an attacker inject data or flood a receiver. Two practical warnings come out of the analysis: never take a random number modulo the size of your range without using rejection sampling, because the distribution becomes lopsided, and never use a plain counter, because the pattern tells an attacker everything about the volume and timing of your traffic.

viz.caption: THE FOUR CATEGORIES OF TRANSIENT NUMERIC IDENTIFIER

items.title: Per-context counter
items.text: A counter per context, started at a random value. Simple, but every context needs a counter in memory and a lost counter can cause reuse.

items.title: Simple PRF-based
items.text: A keyed offset per context plus one shared counter. No per-context state, but the shared counter leaks how many identifiers were issued overall.

items.title: Double-PRF
items.text: A keyed offset per context plus a second keyed function that picks a bucket for the counter, splitting the increment space so traffic analysis is much harder.

items.label: Network activity correlation
items.desc: A predictable value lets an observer link activity within a context, and across networks if the value never changes.

items.label: Information leakage
items.desc: A shared increasing counter reveals how many identifiers have been issued, and so how much traffic a host has produced.

items.label: Fingerprinting
items.desc: Sampling the values can reveal the generating algorithm and its parameters, and with them the operating system.

items.label: Exploitation of semantics
items.desc: An identifier that carries meaning, such as a vendor prefix, narrows the space an attacker has to search.

items.label: Exploitation of collisions
items.desc: A collision can cause a hard failure, and an attacker able to force collisions one after another can turn that into a denial of service.

items.label: Injection attacks
items.desc: Protocols that validate packets with sequence numbers alone can be fed forged data; unpredictability is a poor defence.

items.label: Cryptanalysis
items.desc: A weak pseudorandom function or a misused key lets an attacker recover the key and predict every later value.
